events.title: The Other Side of Geneva: A Matter of Protocol
events.body:
After days of combat in Cyprus, the First Geneva Conference has begun, primarily to establish a lasting ceasefire and take the first steps toward peace. By the end of the first day, the delegations have already made their positions clear, and whether the conference will result in lasting peace is still uncertain, but our delegation has certainly witnessed some bizarre moments!

In fact, problems began before the conference had even started. On July 25, Reşat Arım, secretary to the Turkish delegation, spotted an issue with the conference hall. The tables had been arranged so that Britain appeared to be presiding over the proceedings, with the Turkish and Greek delegations seated beneath its authority. He immediately went to confront D'Outremont, the United Nations protocol chief.

"We have merely rented this hall from the United Nations! We are paying for everything, the hall, the interpreters, the communications. You cannot tell us how to sit! Anyone looking at this arrangement would think Britain was presiding over the Turkish and Greek delegations!"

D'Outremont was utterly confused. How were they going to move the tables? The conference was about to start, and they would need carpenters to rearrange the furniture and technicians to adjust the equipment. Arım, however, was determined that the seating arrangement would not remain as it was.

"Who elected Britain president of this conference? This hall will be changed!"

Carpenters entered the conference hall and moved the tables into a diagonal arrangement with equal spacing between the three delegations, all while the delegates stood by and watched. Unfortunately, the arrangement still wasn't quite right, resulting in carpenters having to move the tables twice more. The conference started half an hour late because of its very first issue, with the carpenters leaving through the doors just as the foreign ministers entered.

The opening session also had a few interesting moments. Coşkun Kırca glanced up toward the balcony and saw several United Nations personnel recording the proceedings with tape recorders. He was furious and immediately summoned Arım, demanding, "Who gave these men permission to record anything? Have them stop recording at once!" The United Nations had intended to prepare a complete transcript of the proceedings, but nobody had thought to ask our delegation for permission.

With the Watergate scandal still dominating the news, nobody wanted confidential diplomatic discussions to be recorded without their knowledge. If we said anything foolish, it could be taken out of context and used to accuse us of selling out our country. The technicians were therefore ordered to stop, and with the recording equipment silenced, the conference could finally proceed.
events.button: Just how İnönü did in Lausanne...

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva: Sleepless Nights
events.body:
Through the following days of the conference, it was unfortunately proving difficult to get any work done, for arguments broke out over where our troops would remain stationed, what the ceasefire meant, who had authority over the Cypriot government, and even the differences between certain diplomatic expressions. Everyone was becoming increasingly exhausted as the negotiations continued through the night, with delegates removing their jackets, loosening their ties, and gradually losing their formerly immaculate appearances.

During one of the most tiring sessions, British diplomat Wiggin suddenly produced a large bottle of whiskey and placed it on the table. The mood changed almost instantly as the delegates began pouring themselves drinks, conversations moved away from Cyprus, and people started talking about their personal experiences. Greek diplomat Dimitrios Bitsios described how he had been arrested on a beach during the recent political upheaval in Greece. Our diplomats realized that the negotiations might continue until sunrise, so they eventually began drinking as well in an effort to keep themselves awake.

It felt more like a tense reunion of old acquaintances than a diplomatic meeting. However, nobody was entirely comfortable with the possibility that they might become intoxicated and weaken their negotiating positions, especially when every clause of the agreement could affect the positions of thousands of soldiers. By the time the sun rose, all three delegations were arguing again, with reddened eyes, disheveled clothes, and barely enough energy to keep talking.

Meanwhile, the journalists covering the conference were experiencing their own peculiar difficulties. Hundreds of reporters waited for news on the lawns surrounding the United Nations Palace, where British television and radio crews organized improvised soccer matches while their northern European colleagues consumed astonishing quantities of beer. As the hours passed, increasingly ridiculous jokes, arguments, and occasional drunken pursuits provided entertainment for the exhausted journalists, even as reports of renewed fighting threatened to turn the conference into the prelude to another war.

At the modest hotel accommodating many of the Turkish journalists, a Greek night attendant named Dimitri had developed a particularly unconventional understanding of international relations. Speaking in his limited Turkish, he asked the journalists to inform him if war between Turkey and Greece was about to resume, explaining that his mother-in-law lived in Thessaloniki and that he would happily provide her address to any Turkish pilots willing to drop a bomb upon it. He even offered to pay for the bomb himself. Dimitri's peculiar humor proved a welcome distraction from the uncertainty surrounding the negotiations, although his generosity was perhaps more useful when he supplied the hungry journalists with bread intended for the following morning's breakfast after the hotel kitchen had closed.
events.button: Sleep deprivation, the excuse! Whiskey, the delight!

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva: An Agreement Nobody Expected
events.body:
By July 28, things had become considerably more serious. We had made good progress toward reaching an agreement when Güneş received a telephone call from Ankara. Prime Minister Ecevit had discovered that the proposed declaration contained language concerning the eventual withdrawal of our troops from Cyprus, and he was deeply dissatisfied with this provision.

"I will not have the flag I personally ordered raised over Kyrenia Castle lowered with my own hands. I will not promise to withdraw the soldiers I sent there!"

Güneş tried to explain that numerous conditions were attached to the provision and that no definite timetable had been established, but Ecevit remained firm. He stated that once an agreement was signed, his government would honor every part of it, making any premature commitment to withdraw our troops politically and militarily unacceptable. The Prime Minister made it clear that the wording had to be removed or the Turkish delegation would withdraw from the conference. This would be the beginning of further stubborn interventions from Ecevit in Ankara, as Güneş would now have to deal not only with the British, Americans, and Greeks, but also with his own government...

However, our diplomats were reluctant to take responsibility for ruining the negotiations, especially after several days of difficult discussions. A plan was therefore devised to present demands that the Greeks would almost certainly refuse. This would allow Turkey to withdraw without appearing responsible for the conference's collapse.

Coşkun Kırca immediately got to work. First, he introduced demands concerning Rauf Denktaş's constitutional authority, which Mavros accepted after considerable argument. Next came a demand that the existence of two de facto autonomous administrations on the island be recognized. The Greek Foreign Minister was initially furious, but Callaghan intervened, the wording was adjusted, and another compromise was reached. Finally, Güneş demanded that the provisions concerning the return of refugees and freedom of movement be removed, only for Mavros to accept yet again.

Our delegation was beginning to realize that its demands were being accepted one after another. The Turkish diplomats had entered the negotiations intending to make an agreement impossible, only to discover that the Greeks were just as determined not to let the conference fail. After further proposals and compromises, Güneş finally turned toward his colleagues in exasperation.

"We cannot get out of here, gentlemen. They have accepted everything. There is nothing else we can do!"

Even the most determined members of the delegation were running out of ideas. It was decided that Ankara should be informed of the unexpected situation, perhaps in the hope that the Prime Minister would reconsider his position. The telephone calls continued, and the exhausted diplomats gradually collapsed into the nearest chairs and sofas as they awaited further instructions.
events.button: Gentlemen, there is nothing we can do but win...

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva: A Minister's Resignation
events.body:
As the days advanced, the conference negotiations were slowly producing considerable progress. However, the greatest crisis was still to come. On the afternoon of July 29, Güneş entered James Callaghan's office for what would become one of the most unpleasant meetings of his political career. The British Foreign Secretary was becoming increasingly angry with Ankara's refusal to accept the proposed withdrawal provisions, and he made little effort to conceal his frustration. He accused Güneş of having no real authority and functioning as little more than a messenger, openly questioning his role in the negotiations.

"You have no role here beyond that of a messenger! If a minister has neither authority nor initiative, he resigns! You are nothing but a telephone receiver!"

Güneş was struggling to remain calm. He pulled at his mustache and bit his lips, trying desperately to restrain his anger. Had almost anyone else spoken to him in such a manner, the ashtray on the table might well have gone flying toward the offending man's head, but two foreign ministers coming to blows would hardly help the negotiations. He replied coldly that there was nothing unusual about governments making decisions on matters of such importance.

However, Callaghan wasn't finished. He stated that he had other business to attend to and would not remain in Geneva indefinitely, giving Turkey until 9:30 the following morning to accept the proposed terms or present an acceptable alternative. Otherwise, Britain would abandon the conference, mobilize NATO and the United Nations, and publicly hold Turkey responsible for its failure.

Güneş left without even shaking his hand. Back at the Turkish mission, his hands were trembling with anger as he gathered the delegation and explained what had happened. Turkey would reject the ultimatum, he declared, and if Callaghan was in such a hurry to leave, he was welcome to do so immediately. He then withdrew into another room with Haluk Ülman and announced that he could no longer continue under these circumstances.

"UNDER THESE CIRCUMSTANCES, I AM RESIGNING!"

Coşkun Kırca was horrified. Withdrawing from the conference now would be disastrous, and he warned Güneş that the entire world would accuse Turkey of barbarism and demand an explanation. The Foreign Minister was utterly exhausted and frustrated, and tears welled up in his eyes as his colleagues pleaded with him to reconsider.

Nevertheless, Güneş remained determined. He wrote out his resignation letter and summoned the telex operator, preparing to relinquish his position in the middle of an international crisis. His colleagues continued trying to dissuade him, with Kırca insisting that abandoning the negotiations after everything they had achieved would be an enormous mistake. Meanwhile, Ülman desperately telephoned Deniz Baykal in Ankara, urging him to intervene before Güneş did something irreversible.

The disagreements between Ankara and Geneva had already strained the delegation considerably, with Güneş repeatedly finding himself caught between the Prime Minister's uncompromising instructions and the delicate diplomatic arrangements negotiated by his advisers. The personal humiliation inflicted by Callaghan had only made matters worse, leaving the Foreign Minister unwilling to endure further insults while simultaneously being held responsible for decisions taken by his own government. Finally, having reached his limit, Güneş announced that he was going to bed and did not wish to speak to anyone, neither the Prime Minister nor Callaghan.

The diplomatic crisis was threatening to become a government crisis as well. Fortunately, while our delegation was trying to prevent its own Foreign Minister from resigning, the British were beginning to realize that their Foreign Secretary might have gone too far. Wiggin approached Kırca and attempted to explain that there had been a misunderstanding.

"There must be some misunderstanding, Mr. Kırca. We have not issued an ultimatum! Callaghan merely mentioned his plane's departure time. He has to attend preparations for the Labour Party conference!"

Having transformed a threat to mobilize NATO and the United Nations against Turkey into an innocent discussion of travel arrangements, the British were now attempting to repair the damage. Kırca was invited to the bar for a drink, where Wiggin continued trying to find a solution. After another round of telephone diplomacy involving Ankara, Athens, London, and Washington, a revised formula was eventually agreed upon. Any potential reduction in armed forces would now depend upon the establishment of suitable political and security conditions, postponing the question of withdrawal considerably. Güneş's resignation was retrieved from the telex operator before it could be transmitted, and he was persuaded to continue the negotiations.

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva: One Last Argument
events.body:
The Geneva Conference was approaching its end, but the absurdities were not quite over. On July 30, just when it seemed that an agreement had finally been reached, a Turkish military representative unexpectedly mentioned the possibility of establishing a ten-kilometer security zone around our positions in Cyprus. The diplomats had specifically instructed the military delegation not to mention any distances, knowing how sensitive the issue was. The Greeks immediately became suspicious, believing that such a zone would allow Turkish troops to exercise effective control over a much larger area of the island.

Mavros was so furious that the conference nearly collapsed once again. "If you have no authority on this matter either, Mr. Güneş, perhaps Ankara should send a general to participate in the next negotiations!" Güneş tried to explain the difficulties of controlling individual soldiers along an uncertain ceasefire line, but the argument grew increasingly heated until Callaghan felt obliged to intervene.

"Gentlemen, please!"

Mavros turned toward him, apparently surprised by the interruption. "Mr. Callaghan, do not worry. We are Mediterranean people. We quarrel now, and a little later we leave arm in arm!"

The atmosphere softened, and after further negotiations and another telephone call to Ankara, it was decided that the question of the security zone would be left for subsequent discussions. Güneş and Mavros finally reached an understanding, with the Greek Foreign Minister extending his hand and declaring, "Agreed, Mr. Güneş."

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva: A Glass of Rakı
events.body:
And so, after five days of arguments, threats, near-resignations, conflicting instructions, endless telephone calls, and considerable quantities of alcohol, the First Geneva Conference finally came to an end. The declaration was signed on July 30 and provided the basis for further negotiations, giving the participants at least a temporary reprieve from the crisis.

Güneş wanted to celebrate. He had survived a conference that had nearly cost him his position, his patience, and perhaps several years of his life, and he enjoyed a drink of rakı afterward with bread topped with tomatoes and cheese. But of course, just like everything else, this produced another controversy, as conservative critics were appalled that a minister representing a country whose soldiers had recently been fighting in Cyprus would celebrate the agreement by drinking alcohol.

Some argued that he should have prayed and expressed gratitude to the fallen soldiers instead. However, as everyone knew, Güneş loved music, jokes, friendly gatherings, and rakı, making the controversy another example of the peculiar standards by which politicians were judged. Apparently, a statesman could negotiate through the night, endure insults from a foreign minister, nearly resign, and help secure an international agreement, only for his seriousness to be questioned because he had enjoyed a drink of rakı afterward.

Five days earlier, three delegations had entered the United Nations Palace to decide the future of Cyprus. They emerged with a declaration, a fragile diplomatic understanding, and a collection of personal arguments that would have seemed unbelievable anywhere outside the world of international diplomacy.

The future of Cyprus remains uncertain. The declaration has not resolved the fundamental disagreements between the parties, and another conference is already being prepared. Nevertheless, after everything that has happened in Geneva, perhaps our delegation can be forgiven for wanting a little rest before returning to the negotiating table.

And perhaps another drink of rakı.
events.button: Hmmm... yes, tomato, hmm, yesss... Cheese... And of course; Rakı!

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva
events.body:
We are finally ready to expand the Second Geneva Conference into a five-party meeting with the arrival of Rauf Denktaş and Glafkos Klerides. However, just as we are about to enter the meeting room, our diplomats realize that the British have arranged for Denktaş and Klerides to sit beneath a single nameplate bearing the title "Republic of Cyprus." Our delegation objects, as the meeting is supposed to recognize the existence of two distinct communities.

However, the British are confused and try to find an alternative, but to no avail. Suggestions range from identifying Klerides as president and Denktaş as the Turkish community's representative to placing them across the table from each other. We make it clear that we will accept nothing less than both men being recognized as representatives of their respective communities. The Greeks refuse, arguing that such an arrangement would suggest the existence of two Cypriot governments.

After much argument over the nameplates, Haluk Ülman loses his patience.

"Come on, let's go. If they refuse to accept it, we might as well wait somewhere else!"

The Turkish delegation grabs its belongings, piles into a car, and heads to a restaurant called Gruyer, well known for its cheese. Hopefully, this dramatic gesture will convince the other delegations to change their minds. However, we quickly realize that nobody is following us. Mavros storms back to his hotel, and Callaghan stays at the United Nations Palace. We continue enjoying our meal, waiting to be begged to return.

Luckily, our delegation has left behind one fully authorized representative. Ömer Akbel, Güneş's young private secretary, has been given the extraordinary responsibility of negotiating the nameplates. He takes this very seriously. Occasionally, he pokes his head around the door and tells anyone nearby that he is ready to negotiate. However, nobody seems interested.

As the afternoon progresses, the United Nations Palace becomes very quiet. The cafeteria closes, the bar closes, and the communications offices close as well. Even the few journalists still there begin falling asleep in the heat. However, Akbel continues waiting in the empty corridors. He can hear his footsteps echoing and occasionally informs anyone unlucky enough to walk past that the fully authorized Turkish representative is available to negotiate!

Callaghan finally realizes that we have gone out for cheese, which does little to ease his frustration. After searching for the Turkish diplomats, he decides to make a statement. During a briefing with British journalists, he accuses Turkey of trying to sabotage the conference. He announces that additional British troops, including Gurkha soldiers, will be sent to Cyprus.

He also states that British aircraft will remain on the island. If British soldiers serving with the United Nations peacekeeping force come under attack, Britain might respond with military action. However, he makes it clear that his statements must not be attributed to him, but to an unnamed senior British official.

One journalist notices how ridiculous the situation is and asks whether the Foreign Secretary has informed Turan Güneş.

"That's your job."

While we are enjoying cheese at a Swiss restaurant and our representative is wandering around an empty palace, the British Foreign Secretary is attempting to threaten Turkey through the newspapers. Eventually, Klerides agrees to continue the meeting without the nameplates, and we return to the conference hall.

After seven long hours, the delegations have finally settled their immediate disagreement. The future of Cyprus is still very uncertain, but at least we can all sit down without arguing over what to put on the nameplates.
events.button: Stand proud Callaghan, for I hate you more than the Junta!

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva: Old Friends and Summer Vacations
events.body:
The negotiations have been brought to life by the arrival of two very interesting figures. Rauf Denktaş and Glafkos Klerides have known each other since their student days and understand each other very well. However, their familiarity with each other's personalities, political difficulties, and negotiating styles has done little to bridge the gap between their two communities.

During the conference, the pair argue and accuse each other over events of the previous decade, the future of the constitution, and what must happen for both communities to live in peace. However, after an extremely long and stressful argument, they are sitting together at the bar, having a drink and chatting in Greek. It appears that their differences have been forgotten!

Klerides begins complaining about an incident in which Turkish soldiers detained a group of Greek Cypriot women and later released them in Nicosia. However, Denktaş, who clearly doesn't want to miss the chance to make a joke, says:

"Look at the greatness of the Turkish soldier! They take your women, and instead of keeping them, they return them to your men!"

The pair continue chatting in a very friendly manner, but their conversation quickly turns serious. Klerides asks Denktaş what he intends to propose at their next meeting, and Denktaş replies, "You'll see tomorrow!" When Klerides admits that he cannot agree with the Turkish position, Denktaş urges him to think over their discussions that evening before they meet again.

Despite their friendship, neither can convince the other to change his political position. However, it is quite a sight to see two people having a huge argument about the future of their island and then enjoying a drink together. Perhaps there is something about being Cypriot that the Turkish, Greek and British delegations cannot understand.

The next morning, another unbelievable misunderstanding occurs within our delegation. While several of us are having breakfast at the Intercontinental Hotel, Haluk Ülman begins talking about his telephone conversation with Prime Minister Ecevit. He then suddenly remembers something and apologizes to Güneş:

"Oh, goodness, Turan! I completely forgot! Bülent told me that Ayşe wants to go on vacation and that her preparations are complete. He said that if your business here is going to take longer, he'll tell her she can leave. I'm sorry, I completely forgot to mention it!"

Güneş, who has been sitting quietly, suddenly becomes very interested.

"When is she supposed to leave?"

Ülman replies that he does not know, as the Prime Minister merely asked him to pass along the message. This makes Güneş even more concerned, and he keeps asking whether the Prime Minister said anything about when she was leaving.

"No, Turan, he didn't! Besides, with everything happening here, I thought it was rather strange that Bülent was concerning himself with Ayşe's vacation. Don't we have more important things to discuss?"

Nermin Güneş, who is also having breakfast, becomes increasingly annoyed by the situation. Why would her daughter discuss going on vacation with the Prime Minister but not with her own mother? She begins complaining to her husband about the children, but Turan doesn't seem to be listening.

"Nermin, darling, just a moment! Haluk, are you absolutely sure he didn't say when she was leaving?"

This has left everyone confused except Güneş. The Foreign Minister suddenly gets up from his seat and rushes upstairs to telephone Ankara. His wife is annoyed, and Ülman cannot understand why there is such a fuss over a harmless message about someone going on a summer vacation.

To the Prime Minister and Foreign Minister, Ayşe going on vacation has nothing to do with an actual vacation. It is a coded message they arranged beforehand to signal that preparations for another military operation in Cyprus are complete, not an order to begin it. The message has arrived at a time when the future of the negotiations looks bleak.

It is unbelievable to think that the fate of an international peace conference depends on a forgotten message about a young woman going on vacation!
events.button: Haluk, for heaven's sake, when is she leaving?!

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva
events.body:
As the Second Geneva Conference heads toward disaster, Prime Minister Ecevit has decided to try one last time to find a diplomatic solution. Following discussions with Henry Kissinger, Ankara has agreed to prepare an alternative to its two-zone federal proposal, creating multiple autonomous Turkish cantons throughout Cyprus. This is intended to demonstrate that Turkey is open to compromise and present the Greeks and Greek Cypriots with an option they may be more willing to accept.

Our diplomats, however, are not too pleased with this. As Denktaş prepares to present his two-zone federal proposal, Güneş has been asked to present the alternative cantonal plan. He is unsure whether the cantons would provide enough security for the Turkish community. Ecmel Barutçu is particularly concerned that the Greeks might accept the deal to prevent another military operation and trap Turkey in lengthy negotiations over the cantons' locations and boundaries.

Güneş repeatedly complains to Haluk Ülman about this possibility.

"What if they actually accept it, Haluk?"

It's a bizarre situation. Our diplomats tried to make the First Geneva Conference fail completely, only for Mavros to accept their increasingly demanding proposals. Now that we are back in the same city, we seem to have developed a strange fear of succeeding diplomatically. Nevertheless, both proposals still need to be presented, beginning with Denktaş's two-zone plan, which he brings to his old friend Klerides.

Unfortunately, Klerides doesn't even want to receive the document officially, as that might make it appear that he is willing to negotiate the partition of the island. Annoyed by all the formalities, Denktaş suggests that he accept it informally instead. He then proceeds to toss the document onto Klerides's lap. The Greek Cypriot leader quickly moves it onto the table, but Denktaş insists that he take it.

They engage in a childlike struggle over the document. Eventually, Denktaş manages to push it into Klerides's hands.

The proposal would divide Cyprus into two areas. Around 34 percent of the island would form an autonomous Turkish region, stretching from the western coast through northern Nicosia toward the Turkish sector of Famagusta. Klerides is shocked and says that he cannot accept the idea, as it would be impossible to explain to the Greek Cypriot population.

"Rauf, I cannot accept this! You are dividing Cyprus in two, and you have even taken the port of Famagusta!"

Denktaş tries to assure him that they can negotiate the exact borders and perhaps come up with a joint arrangement for the port. Klerides is adamant that he cannot return to Nicosia having accepted the division of the island; his people would regard him as a traitor. Despite being friends, they cannot reach an agreement, and after a long discussion, the proposal remains unaccepted.

We discover that delivering the alternative cantonal proposal is almost as difficult. The Greek representatives are nowhere to be found at their hotel, and Klerides is missing as well. The Turkish diplomats spend much of the day trying to find someone willing to receive the document. Eventually, they find a Greek diplomat who accepts it against a signature, while another copy is slipped under Klerides's hotel room door.

After days of diplomatic discussions, we have reached a very strange position. One proposal has practically been shoved into someone's hands, while another has been slipped under a hotel door.

As evening approaches, Güneş and his colleagues wait to hear whether the Greeks will reject the proposals or attempt to delay negotiations by requesting more time.

Somewhere in our delegation, there is a slightly strange hope that the Greeks won't make the terrible mistake of accepting our own proposal.
events.button: I mean obviously, they won't accept it... Right?

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva: Same Old Arguments
events.body:
By August 13, the atmosphere has become extremely tense. Ankara wants answers regarding its proposals, the Greeks are requesting more time to consult their government, and the British are trying to salvage the talks. The journalists are beginning to tire, but the delegates seem to have endless stamina for repeating their arguments.

The strange atmosphere is evident in the Intercontinental Hotel lobby, where both Güneş and Mavros have begun giving updates to journalists. The Turkish Foreign Minister is surrounded by foreign reporters asking about Ankara's intentions. Only a few meters away, his Greek counterpart is speaking to another group of journalists and accusing Turkey of trying to impose its proposals by force. Occasionally, one of the ministers gestures toward the other while explaining his position, leaving two foreign ministers arguing through journalists despite standing only a few steps apart.

Denktaş and Klerides have begun negotiating again, but their first disagreement concerns the acceptance of a document. After refusing to receive Denktaş's proposal the previous day, Klerides has brought a written counterproposal of his own. Unfortunately, Denktaş seems determined to return the favor and asks why he should accept a document from someone who has repeatedly claimed that the conference has no authority to discuss Cyprus's constitutional future.

After a brief struggle over the paper, Denktaş agrees to receive the proposal and begins reading it. Klerides is offering a revised constitutional arrangement granting greater administrative autonomy to the Turkish community, but without accepting geographical separation. However, Denktaş quickly realizes that many of the terms resemble those the Turkish Cypriots had already requested during earlier intercommunal negotiations.

"Why, these are the very same rights we asked you for during the intercommunal negotiations, and you refused to grant them!"

Klerides argues that this demonstrates his good faith. However, Denktaş is unwilling to accept terms that do not guarantee his community's security. Once again, they argue over autonomy, territory, and the risk of renewed violence. Neither can persuade the other.

Haluk Ülman is trying to reassure those worried about the international pressure on Turkey. When journalist Mehmet Ali Birand warns him that confronting Britain and the Western powers could prove more difficult than they think, Ülman replies by recalling the CHP reformists' struggle against İsmet İnönü.

"We are people who have struggled to get where we are today! We fought İnönü and overthrew him!"

Birand is quite surprised and points out that an international confrontation with Britain is hardly the same as a fight for leadership within one's own party. However, Ülman remains confident, having already experienced a major political struggle and seeing little reason to be intimidated by another.

"No, Mehmet Ali. You're still young, and you cannot understand. Overthrowing İnönü is harder than fighting Britain!"

As the delegates prepare to return to the conference hall, George Mavros provides one last moment of accidental comedy. Walking down the corridor, he suddenly grabs a young diplomat's arm and begins speaking to him in Greek, apparently expecting an answer. The unfortunate man, Engin Ansay, is one of our own delegates and has absolutely no idea why the Greek Foreign Minister is addressing him.

Ansay finally interrupts.

"Mr. Mavros, the Greek delegation is entering the conference hall over there."

Mavros looks at him more carefully and realizes his mistake. Just a few days earlier, he had commented on how similar Turks and Greeks are, saying that they have more in common with each other than with the British. Apparently, he isn't quite as good at telling them apart as he thought!

The delegations sit down, and the talks resume. As always, there is frustration, mistrust, and the same old arguments. However, with the deadline set by Ankara looming, there is less room for another diplomatic misunderstanding.
events.button: Overthrowing İnönü was harder than fighting Britain!

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva: How to End a Conference?
events.body:
The Second Geneva Conference is coming to a close, and we have been told that since the Greeks are unwilling to accept Turkey's proposals, the talks must be brought to an end. Ankara is already prepared for another operation in Cyprus, so Güneş needs to conclude the conference without causing confusion. However, there is one strange problem that the Foreign Minister has never encountered before.

How do you end an international peace conference?

Güneş looks around at his professional diplomats to see if they have any ideas.

"What am I supposed to do now, gentlemen? I don't know how to walk out of a conference! We're village boys, after all. Do I slam the door behind me? Throw my papers onto the table? Someone tell me how this is supposed to work!"

Unfortunately, the professional diplomats do not have a particularly helpful answer. They have focused more on negotiating international agreements and have not considered the dramatic side of ending the talks. Güneş is unsure whether he should simply stand up and walk out, deliver an angry speech, or declare that the conference is over.

Another issue becomes apparent. The final meeting is scheduled to begin in the evening, and Ankara needs the negotiations to continue until the appropriate time before officially ending. After days of debating practically every possible issue concerning Cyprus, Güneş faces an entirely new problem.

"Good heavens, what am I supposed to talk about for all those hours?"

The delegates resume debating federation, the withdrawal of forces, and the Greek request for more time. Klerides states that he cannot agree to such constitutional changes without consulting his community, while Mavros argues that Greece cannot accept an agreement imposed under military pressure. Klerides requests 48 hours, while Mavros asks for 36 to consult Athens. Güneş explains that Turkey is asking for a political commitment, not agreement on every detail, but neither side is willing to give Ankara the answer it wants.

Our diplomats begin discussing how they can fill the remaining time without creating further problems. Someone suggests persuading Rauf Denktaş to give a long speech. As he knows a great deal about Cyprus's complicated history, this seems like a good idea.

Denktaş is happy to help, but asks:

"Of course I'll speak, but what am I supposed to talk about?"

"Start from the 1500s!"

"How can I start from there? We weren't the oppressed side back then!"

Despite this, Denktaş gives a lengthy speech about the history of the Cyprus question, the Turkish Cypriot experience, and why his community demands security. He speaks for nearly an hour, and eventually Haluk Ülman has to send a note through Osman Örek asking him to stop talking.

Ironically, we have been complaining throughout the conference that the Greeks are deliberately dragging out the talks, but now we are desperately trying to keep the conference going ourselves.

As the evening goes on, tensions rise. Callaghan is still trying to persuade the Turkish delegation to allow more time, while Klerides insists that he is merely asking for 48 hours to consider the proposals. The disagreement has now reached the point where they are no longer debating the agreement itself, but whether failing to give an answer counts as a rejection.

Callaghan suggests another coffee break, prompting Güneş to glance anxiously at his watch. He agrees, but insists that the break must not last too long. The British Foreign Secretary cannot resist remarking on how accommodating Güneş becomes when it suits him, apparently unaware of just how concerned the Turkish minister is about the time.

Coşkun Kırca attempts another intervention. He approaches a Greek diplomat he knows well and asks whether the Greek delegation has understood Kissinger's latest statement about security and autonomy for the Turkish Cypriot community. The diplomat insists that Washington opposes another military operation, but Kırca warns him that Ankara has interpreted the statement rather differently.

"I am telling you how Turkey has interpreted it. And the people making that interpretation are the very same people who will decide whether the army advances!"

The warning is passed on to Mavros, but it does not change his position. Arguments continue, and the hours pass. Our delegates grow increasingly concerned as the clock above the conference hall doors ticks away, fearing that the meeting will continue beyond the military timetable.

Güneş tries one last time to obtain a definite answer. He summarizes Turkey's three principal demands: a geographically based federal arrangement, the transfer of territory to Turkish Cypriot administration, and the establishment of a security zone.

Klerides again asks for 48 hours, emphasizing that he is not formally rejecting Turkey's proposals. Mavros supports the request, and Callaghan insists that diplomatic options remain.

Güneş looks at the clock and replies that the answers are insufficient. From Turkey's perspective, the conference has come to an end, and everyone must accept responsibility.

Once again, the British Foreign Secretary tries to keep the conference going. He asks whether they will meet again on Thursday morning. Klerides agrees, Mavros agrees, and Denktaş says that he will attend as long as Turkey does.

They all look to Güneş.

Güneş does not reply.

After days of arguments, interruptions, threats, and endless diplomacy, the man who was worrying about how to end an international conference has finally found the answer: he says nothing.
events.button: I suppose that's how you end a conference.

events.title: The Other Side of Geneva
events.body:
As the Second Geneva Conference approaches its conclusion, the atmosphere surrounding the Turkish delegation has become increasingly hostile. Foreign journalists pursue our representatives wherever they go, protests against Turkey are becoming more frequent, and the possibility of renewed fighting in Cyprus has put everyone under considerable pressure. While Güneş and Denktaş enjoy security protection, the other members of the delegation must generally look after themselves.

However, İsmail Müftüoğlu, the MSP's political representative, has become increasingly concerned about the situation. He is convinced that there is a risk of assassination, so he arranges for a pistol to be brought to him and carries it during the final days of the conference. His colleagues are consequently treated to the unusual sight of a member of parliament attending international peace negotiations with a gun concealed in his clothing.

As the conference comes to an end, the delegation leaves the United Nations Palace to find a crowd of protesters outside. They are shouting anti-Turkish and anti-American slogans. Although Swiss police officers are present, the delegates must still pass in front of the demonstrators to reach their hotel.

Müftüoğlu quickly draws his pistol and sits low in the back of the car, on the side closest to the protesters. Güneş sits in the middle, with Haluk Ülman on the other side, apparently unaware of just how seriously Müftüoğlu is taking the situation.

The car slowly drives past the crowd, with Müftüoğlu keeping his pistol ready in case anyone tries to attack them. Fortunately, the protesters do not recognize the occupants, and the delegation reaches its destination safely.

The Turkish delegation stays in Geneva for another day before departing on August 15. However, during the flight home, Müftüoğlu reveals a completely different side of his personality. He spends much of the journey writing poems and handing them to Rauf Denktaş.

Denktaş seems pleased by the unexpected poems and offers to have them read on Bayrak Radio.

After threatening suicide over Güneş's resignation, arguing with members of his own government, criticizing the drinking habits of professional diplomats, and carrying a pistol past a crowd of protesters, Müftüoğlu ends his diplomatic adventure as an enthusiastic poet.

It is difficult to imagine what the delegation might have experienced had the negotiations lasted another week.
events.button: From a pistol to poetry. What a diplomat!

insertion:
The Second Geneva Conference has barely begun, yet the delegates are already arguing over which problem should be discussed first. The Greeks insist that the ceasefire lines must be properly established before anything else, while our delegation demands the immediate evacuation of Turkish villages still under Greek Cypriot control. James Callaghan, increasingly frustrated with the endless arguments over priorities, finally suggests that both matters be discussed simultaneously, or perhaps that they should simply draw lots to decide which one comes first! The suggestion produces some laughter, but does little to resolve the disagreements.

The following morning, Ecmel Barutçu finds himself presiding over a committee tasked with establishing procedures for evacuating the occupied Turkish villages. Unfortunately, he cannot quite understand why such a committee is necessary in the first place, arguing that Mavros could simply telephone Cyprus and order the villages evacuated. The British insist on consulting United Nations representatives, while the Greeks propose exchanging lists of villages through Athens and Nicosia before determining which should be evacuated.

"Why are we wasting time with all these lists? If you want the villages evacuated, then evacuate them!"

When the British insist that Callaghan expects a report from the committee, Barutçu threatens to walk out rather than participate in what he increasingly suspects is an elaborate delaying tactic. The British diplomats hurriedly attempt to calm him, explaining that Callaghan has ordered them to produce a report, even if discussions take all night. By the time the meeting ends, everyone has spent hours discussing the evacuation of Turkish villages without actually evacuating a single one.
